summary.headline: A world leader in coconut-shell carbon having a boom year, but the price is over three times fair value and the boom is being paid for with debt
summary.text: Haycarb PLC (HAYC.N0000), 68% owned by Hayleys, makes activated carbon from coconut-shell charcoal in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia and soon the Philippines (58,500 tonnes a year, about 16% of the world market by its own count). Its carbons go into gold mining, water and air purification and, increasingly, batteries and supercapacitors. Demand is booming: revenue rose 55% to Rs 67.1bn in 2025/26 and another 42% in the six months to September 2026, when EPS doubled to Rs 8.41 (Rs 4.71 in the September quarter alone). It passes 3 of the 4 business tests (good returns over several years, debt under equity, profit every year), but fails the cash test: profit isn't turning into cash. Charcoal stocks and debtors absorbed Rs 13.4bn in 2025/26 and another Rs 8.5bn of stock in the half year, so operating cash was −Rs 5.6bn and −Rs 1.9bn, and net debt jumped from Rs 5.0bn to Rs 25.5bn in eighteen months, mostly short-term loans. On a provisional beta of 1.33 (cost of equity 21.9%), the P/E, price-to-book and residual-income methods give a fair value of about Rs 64.80. At Rs 224 (a mid-November web price) the share is 2.1x NAV of Rs 107.67 and 13.7x trailing EPS of Rs 16.35; the price implies a cost of equity of about 10–12%, below the 12.24% government bond. I'd buy at up to about Rs 55 and treat under Rs 48.60 as a strong buy. Category 2 (watch list): a good business, priced far above the buy level. The beta is the biggest uncertainty: at 1.05 (US sector figure) fair value would be about Rs 75–80, still a third of the price.

valuation.note: Fair value averages the 30/50/20-weighted values of three methods (P/E Rs 69.12, justified P/B Rs 67.80, residual income Rs 57.44), all from scripts/valuation.py using the saved modelInputs; 0.60x NAV. Discount rate: cost of equity 21.9% from beta 1.33 (provisional). A whole-company DCF was run as a cross-check but isn't weighted (see the methods note).

methodReadings.reading: Last 12 months. 12.3% in 2025/26 and 14% in 2024/25; 17% on average over five years and 16% over ten, with a 26% peak in 2022/23.
On trailing EPS of Rs 16.35. Year-end P/E was 2.9–9.0x over the last five years. At a 21.9% cost of equity the justified forward P/E is about 4x.
Rs 4.07 for 2025/26, a third of profit, but paid while operating cash was negative: in effect paid from borrowing. Dividend at risk if stocks don't unwind.
CAPM with a country premium, beta 1.33 (provisional, relevered for the new debt).
0.80x owners' equity at September 2026 (0.15x in March 2025); about 2.4x the last 12 months' EBITDA. Mostly short-term loans funding charcoal stocks.

Not weighted. On normalised cash, the business is worth about Rs 29bn at WACC in the base case, barely more than its net debt, because so much of today's debt funds stock that a DCF treats as permanent.

models.name: P/E method
models.comment: EPS for the year to March 2027 of Rs 15.0 / 17.5 / 19.0 (H1 Rs 8.41 plus a second half of Rs 6.6 / 9.1 / 10.6; the September quarter alone was Rs 4.71) times 3.4 / 4.1 / 4.8: the forward P/E justified at the cost of equity when growth is paid for (payout = 1 − long-run growth ÷ ROE; long-run ROE 12 / 16 / 19%, growth 4 / 5 / 6%). The run-rate is Rs 18.84 (September quarter × 4; last 12 months Rs 16.35): base is 7% below it because gold-carbon demand and charcoal prices are at a peak; bear is 20% below for margins slipping back towards 2025/26 levels. These P/Es are far below the market's 13.7x because a 21.9% cost of equity leaves little room for growth to add value.

models.name: Justified price to book
models.comment: (Long-run ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth) × NAV Rs 107.67 (30 Sep 2026): ROE 12% / 16% / 19%, growth 4% / 5% / 6%, cost of equity 23.4% / 21.9% / 20.4%. Haycarb's ROE averaged 17% over five years and 16% over ten (12% to 26%), so 16% is the base. Below 1x book in every case because even the bull ROE is under the cost of equity.

models.name: Residual income
models.comment: Book value Rs 107.67 (September); ROE moving in a straight line from 16% (last 12 months, Rs 16.35 ÷ average NAV) to 12% / 16% / 19% over ten years; 33% payout (2025/26: Rs 4.07 of Rs 12.18); cost of equity 23.4% / 21.9% / 20.4%; after year ten the excess return grows at 4% / 5% / 6%. Lower than price to book because the excess return is negative from the start and book keeps growing.

modelsNote: Haycarb is a manufacturer, so a whole-company DCF would normally lead. It is shown only as a cross-check here: operating cash was negative in 2025/26 and the half year (a Rs 13.4bn and Rs 8.5bn working-capital build), so the DCF had to start from normalised cash (after-tax operating profit less maintenance, owners' share: Rs 3.0 / 5.1 / 6.0bn), and with Rs 25.5bn of net debt to subtract it swings from Rs −45 to Rs 66 a share (base Rs 13; 64% of the value after year 5). The weighted methods are the P/E, justified price to book and residual income, all at the same 21.9% cost of equity. Growth check: assumed 3% / 7% / 10% a year for five years. The calculator's supported rate (52%, from 2025/26 reinvestment × 16.2% return on capital) is inflated by the stock build, so the share of profit kept × ROE (66.6% × 12.3% = 8.2%) is the fairer test: all three scenarios are within 2 points of it, and the Philippines plant (+13% capacity, 2027/28) supports the bull. Maintenance capex range Rs 1.21–3.51bn (the bear is the two-year average of capex booked, inflated by growth projects); the report names Rs 2.69bn of 2025/26 capex as expansion, so 2025/26 capex was mostly growth. Dividends exceeded cash after maintenance capex in 2025/26: dividend at risk if stocks don't unwind. Method values come from scripts/valuation.py, so the What if? panel reproduces them.

fullText:
**Summary**

Haycarb PLC (HAYC.N0000), 68% owned by Hayleys, makes activated carbon from coconut-shell charcoal in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia and soon the Philippines (58,500 tonnes a year, about 16% of the world market by its own count). Its carbons go into gold mining, water and air purification and, increasingly, batteries and supercapacitors. Demand is booming: revenue rose 55% to Rs 67.1bn in 2025/26 and another 42% in the six months to September 2026, when EPS doubled to Rs 8.41 (Rs 4.71 in the September quarter alone). It passes 3 of the 4 business tests (good returns over several years, debt under equity, profit every year), but fails the cash test: profit isn't turning into cash. Charcoal stocks and debtors absorbed Rs 13.4bn in 2025/26 and another Rs 8.5bn of stock in the half year, so operating cash was −Rs 5.6bn and −Rs 1.9bn, and net debt jumped from Rs 5.0bn to Rs 25.5bn in eighteen months, mostly short-term loans. On a provisional beta of 1.33 (cost of equity 21.9%), the P/E, price-to-book and residual-income methods give a fair value of about Rs 64.80. At Rs 224 (a mid-November web price) the share is 2.1x NAV of Rs 107.67 and 13.7x trailing EPS of Rs 16.35; the price implies a cost of equity of about 10–12%, below the 12.24% government bond. I'd buy at up to about Rs 55 and treat under Rs 48.60 as a strong buy. Category 2 (watch list): a good business, priced far above the buy level. The beta is the biggest uncertainty: at 1.05 (US sector figure) fair value would be about Rs 75–80, still a third of the price.

**The business**

Haycarb turns coconut-shell charcoal into activated carbon: eight factories (Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines from 2027/28), 58,500 tonnes a year of capacity running at 91%, over 1,500 products and about 16% of the world market for this kind of carbon. Main uses: gold recovery, water and air purification, and now energy storage (silicon-carbon battery anodes and supercapacitors). A small environmental-engineering arm, Puritas, builds water and wastewater plants in Sri Lanka and the Maldives. Hayleys owns 67.73%.

**What happened**

2025/26 (audited): revenue Rs 67.08bn (+55%), but gross margin fell from 27.9% to 19.9% because charcoal prices rose faster than carbon prices. Operating profit Rs 6.93bn, profit attributable Rs 3.62bn, EPS Rs 12.18 (Rs 12.10), ROE 12.3%, dividend Rs 4.07.

April–September 2026: revenue Rs 40.56bn (+42%), gross margin back up to 21.9% (23.8% in the September quarter), operating profit Rs 4.98bn (+92%), EPS Rs 8.41 (Rs 4.24). The September quarter alone earned Rs 4.71 a share. Two interim dividends so far: Rs 0.75 and Rs 1.00.

The weak point is cash. Stock rose from Rs 15.2bn (March 2025) to Rs 31.5bn (September 2026), as management built buffer stocks of charcoal at high prices, and debtors grew with sales. Operating cash flow was −Rs 5.58bn in 2025/26 and −Rs 1.88bn in the half year, while capex was Rs 4.28bn and Rs 4.87bn. So net debt (with leases and a Rs 1.8bn loan from a related party) rose from Rs 5.0bn to Rs 17.2bn to Rs 25.5bn, almost all of it short-term. Interest doubled, and currency losses on loans added Rs 0.31bn in the half.

**Business tests (3 of 4: good)**

- Returns: pass, narrowly. ROE averaged 17% over five years and is about 16% on the last 12 months, but was 14% and 12.3% in the last two full years.
- Debt: pass. Net debt 0.80x owners' equity and about 2.4x EBITDA, up from 0.15x in March 2025.
- Steady profit: pass. Profit in every one of the last ten years.
- Cash: fail. Five years of operating cash (Rs 9.7bn) against Rs 23.2bn of profit; negative for the last 18 months; dividends paid from borrowing.

**Required return**

Beta 1.33 (provisional): Damodaran's global specialty-chemicals unlevered beta 1.04, relevered for net debt of 38% of market value. Cost of equity 8.24% + 1.33 × 10.28% = 21.9% (bear 23.4%, bull 20.4%); WACC 17.2%. With the US sector beta it would be 1.05 and 19.0%.

**Valuation**

| Method | Bear | Base | Bull | Weighted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P/E | 51.55 | 71.19 | 90.28 | 69.12 |
| Justified P/B | 44.40 | 70.08 | 97.20 | 67.80 |
| Residual income | 38.68 | 58.20 | 83.70 | 57.44 |
| **Fair value** | | | | **64.79** |

Buy price Rs 55.07 (15% below), strong buy Rs 48.59 (25% below). Scenarios weighted 30/50/20.

- P/E: EPS for 2026/27 of Rs 15.0 / 17.5 / 19.0 × justified P/E 3.4 / 4.1 / 4.8. Base is 7% below the September-quarter run-rate (Rs 18.84) because gold-carbon demand and charcoal prices look like a peak.
- Price to book and residual income: long-run ROE 12% / 16% / 19% against a 21.9% cost of equity, so value stays below book (Rs 107.67).
- Whole-company DCF (not weighted): on normalised cash of Rs 3.0 / 5.1 / 6.0bn, growth 3% / 7% / 10% for five years, at WACC, less Rs 25.5bn of net debt: Rs −45 / 13 / 66 a share. It shows how much of the business's value the debt now takes up.

Growth check: assumed 3% / 7% / 10%; profit kept × ROE supports about 8.2% (the calculator's 52% is distorted by the stock build). The Philippines plant adds about 13% to capacity from 2027/28.

**Why the market price is so much higher**

At Rs 224 the market pays 2.1x book and 13.7x trailing earnings: it is pricing either a much lower risk (a cost of equity around 10–13%, at or below the government bond yield) or ROE staying well above 20% for years. Neither fits Haycarb's record (ROE 12–26%, cyclical with gold prices and charcoal costs) or its new debt.

**Buy plan (500 shares)**

200 shares up to Rs 64.80, 150 up to Rs 55.05, 150 up to Rs 48.55: about Rs 28,500, average Rs 57.00. Not realistic soon: the share traded Rs 110–225 this year and was last near these levels in 2022/23.

**What would change the view**

Higher: a lower beta after the January refresh; stocks turning back into cash and net debt falling; ROE holding near 18–20%. Lower: gold prices falling; charcoal staying dear while carbon prices fall; losses on the Rs 31.5bn of stock; more short-term debt; Philippines delays.

**Management and plans**

Demand for its carbons is booming and capacity is being added in Sri Lanka and the Philippines, but the growth is being paid for with short-term loans while costly charcoal stocks pile up; whether that stock turns back into cash is the thing to watch. 2026/27 targets: revenue growth over 5%, ROE over 10%, gearing under 50%; all on track at the half year (gearing about 44%). Spending in 2025/26: Rs 1,425mn on energy-storage carbon capacity, Rs 1,264mn on value-added capacity; the Philippines plant (7,500 tonnes) is due to start in phases from 2027/28.

**Shareholders**

Hayleys PLC controls Haycarb with 67.73%, unchanged; the EPF holds 4.45%. The September quarter saw steady buying: GF Capital Global (+0.9mn), Dr Dilesh Jayanntha (+0.39mn), the Managing Director (+0.37mn) and HNB's Senfin Growth Fund (+0.30mn); no big holder sold. Public holding 30.73% (9,255 holders).

**Uncertain**

The price is a web snapshot (Rs 224), not a CSE close. The beta uses a global sector figure because Damodaran's emerging-markets file couldn't be opened, and no local 5-year beta was found. The interim doesn't split out the related-party loan, so the March figure (Rs 1.8bn) is used for September. The September interim's cover page wrongly says 'three months ended 30th June 2026'; the statements inside are for six months to September.
